trials.answer:
BFS finds a shortest path in an unweighted graph because it explores vertices in order of their distance from the source: first all vertices one edge away, then all vertices two edges away, and so on. Thus, the first time it reaches a vertex, it has found a path using the fewest edges. DFS may follow a long path before exploring a shorter one, so its first path to a vertex need not be shortest.

With an adjacency-list representation, BFS takes **O(V + E)** time. With a visited set, its worst-case auxiliary space is **O(V)**: the visited set and queue can each hold up to O(V) vertices. DFS can also take **O(V + E)** time and O(V) worst-case auxiliary space; it does not guarantee shortest paths.

trials.answer:
BFS explores the graph level by level, so the first time it reaches a vertex, it has found a path with the fewest edges. In an unweighted graph, every edge has equal cost; any shorter path would have been explored in an earlier level. DFS can follow a long path first and reach the same vertex without finding its shortest path.

With an adjacency-list representation, BFS takes **O(V + E)** time and **O(V)** worst-case auxiliary space for the visited set, queue, and related traversal state.

trials.answer: Marking a vertex when it’s enqueued ensures each vertex enters the queue only once, preventing duplicate work and keeping the queue bounded by O(V). In an unweighted graph, the first time BFS discovers a vertex is along a shortest path, so its distance and parent are already final. Marking only when dequeuing can let multiple vertices enqueue the same neighbor before it’s processed, requiring duplicate handling and potentially overwriting its parent.
